passage:
"It's ugly!" Kamal crumpled the paper into a ball.
"Kamal, that was your card for Ravi," said Damini Ma'am. "The flower leaned a little, that's all."
"It's crooked. I hate it."
"Would you like to try one more? I'll sit with you."
"No. I don't want to."
"Ravi's party is tomorrow."
"Then I won't give him one." Kamal folded his arms and turned to face the wall.
Damini Ma'am smoothed the ball flat and put it in her drawer. Kamal did not look.

qa.q: What did Kamal say about his drawing?
qa.a: He said it was ugly and crooked.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he crumpled the paper, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was disappointed and upset. He crumpled the card, folded his arms and turned to the wall, so the crooked flower mattered a lot to him.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help Kamal, and why?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher to help him draw a first line, or turn the leaning flower into a flower in the wind. Then the card would not have to be perfect to be finished.

qa.q: How does Damini Ma'am see the crooked flower, and why did she keep the paper?
qa.a: She sees a small lean, not a failure. Smoothing the paper and keeping it leaves a way open for Kamal to come back to it.

grounding: A crooked drawing makes the child crumple it and refuse another card, so the wish for a perfect result stops the effort.

passage: Note, Tuesday, Sunflower class. Ishita worked hard this morning on a card for Sangeeta's birthday. She drew a house, but the roof tilted and one wall leaned. She stared at it, crushed the paper into a ball, and said, "It's ugly." I offered a new sheet and she shook her head, arms folded. "I'm not making one." She sat under the table for a while. At circle time Sangeeta got cards from the others; Ishita watched and looked at the floor. Tomorrow I will draw something wobbly myself, to show her that mistakes are allowed, and I'll tell her mother at pickup today.

qa.q: What did Ishita draw for Sangeeta's card?
qa.a: She drew a house, but the roof tilted and one wall leaned.

qa.q: What might Ishita have been feeling as Sangeeta got the other cards?
qa.a: Looking at the floor suggests she felt sad and maybe ashamed that she had nothing to give after crushing hers.

qa.q: What else could Ishita try when a drawing comes out crooked?
qa.a: She could keep the crooked house and add to it, or try again on the new sheet; wanting it perfect is what made her stop.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Ishita's giving up?
qa.a: The note-writer sees that fear of a crooked result stopped her, and plans to draw something wobbly on purpose so she learns mistakes are allowed.

grounding: Shows a child crumpling a crooked drawing and refusing to try again, so the wish for a perfect card stops the effort.

passage: Dhruv bhaiya's birthday was today, and Preeti wanted her card ready before the school bus dropped him at the kasba stand. She sat on the charpai in the courtyard and drew a kite. The string came out bent and the kite was lopsided. Preeti looked at it, scrunched it tight, and threw it by the buffalo trough. "It's ugly." Dadi held out another page from an old notebook. Preeti turned her face away. "No more." When Dhruv came home, he got a laddoo from Dadi and a hug from Maa, but nothing from Preeti. She hid behind the door, wishing she had kept the bent kite.

qa.q: Where did Preeti throw the crumpled card?
qa.a: She threw it by the buffalo trough.

qa.q: What does Preeti hiding behind the door suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems sorry and a bit ashamed, wishing she had kept the bent kite so she had something to give Dhruv.

qa.q: What would you change first for Preeti?
qa.a: Help her see that a lopsided kite is still a gift, or gently get her to try Dadi's fresh page; one more go could have left her with a card.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see getting nothing from Preeti?
qa.a: Dhruv doesn't know about the bent kite, so he might only notice that his little sister is hiding and wonder why.

grounding: Illustrates a child crumpling a crooked drawing and refusing another try, so the wish for perfection leaves her with no card.
